Demographics of India :: part 02 :: chunk_0001
India remains a relatively young country, though it is undergoing a gradual demographic transition. As of 2024, the [median age](/wiki/Median_age "Median age") is approximately 29.8 years,[[15]](#cite_note-15) compared to 40.2 in China. The [United Nations Population Fund](/wiki/United_Nations_Population_Fund "United Nations Population Fund") (UNFPA) estimates that 68% of the population is between 15 and 64 years old, creating a potential "[demographic dividend](/wiki/Demographic_dividend "Demographic dividend")" where a large working-age population can drive economic growth.[[16]](#cite_note-16) However, the number of children is declining; the under-5 population peaked in 2007 and the under-15 cohort peaked in 2011.[[17]](#cite_note-17)

Between 1975 and 2010, the population doubled to 1.2 billion. While the population continues to grow, the rate has slowed significantly from 2.3% annually (1972–1983) to roughly 0.89% in 2023. Current projections suggest the population will reach 1.7 billion by 2050.

India is highly diverse, hosting thousands of ethnic groups and four major [language families](/wiki/Language_family "Language family"): [Indo-European](/wiki/Indo-European_languages "Indo-European languages"), [Dravidian](/wiki/Dravidian_languages "Dravidian languages"), [Austroasiatic](/wiki/Austroasiatic_languages "Austroasiatic languages"), and [Tibeto-Burman](/wiki/Sino-Tibetan_languages "Sino-Tibetan languages").[[18]](#cite_note-18) The country also includes linguistic isolates such as [Nihali](/wiki/Nihali_language "Nihali language") and [Burushaski](/wiki/Burushaski "Burushaski"), and distinct minority communities including [Anglo-Indians](/wiki/Anglo-Indians "Anglo-Indians") and [Siddi](/wiki/Siddi "Siddi").

The [human sex ratio](/wiki/Human_sex_ratio "Human sex ratio") has shown an upward trend after decades of decline, reaching 943 females per 1,000 males in 2011 and estimated at 1,060 males per 1,000 females (approx. 944 females/1000 males) in 2023.[[19]](#cite_note-2011_Provisional_population_tables-19)

See also: [Economic history of India](/wiki/Economic_history_of_India "Economic history of India")

Maltese architecture has been influenced by many different Mediterranean cultures and British architecture over its history.[[309]](#cite_note-311) The first settlers on the island constructed [Ġgantija](/wiki/%C4%A0gantija "Ġgantija"), one of the oldest manmade freestanding structures in the world. The Neolithic temple builders (3800–2500 BC) endowed the numerous temples of Malta and Gozo with intricate bas-relief designs.

The Roman period introduced highly decorative mosaic floors, marble colonnades, and classical statuary, remnants of which are beautifully preserved and presented in the Roman Domus, a country villa just outside the walls of [Mdina](/wiki/Mdina "Mdina"). The early Christian frescoes that decorate the [catacombs](/wiki/Catacombs "Catacombs") beneath Malta reveal a propensity for eastern, [Byzantine](/wiki/Byzantine "Byzantine") tastes. These tastes continued to inform the endeavours of [medieval](/wiki/Medieval "Medieval") Maltese artists, but they were increasingly influenced by the [Romanesque](/wiki/Romanesque_art "Romanesque art") and [Southern French Gothic](/wiki/Southern_French_Gothic "Southern French Gothic") movements.

A survey of experts classified the Shiba Inu as having "high aggression, high reactivity and medium trainability".[[13]](#cite_note-TAKEUCHI_MORI_2006_pp._789–796-13) A possible explanation for this and other observed behaviour is that the Shiba Inu is more closely related to the [wolf](/wiki/Wolf "Wolf") than domesticated dogs from other countries.[[14]](#cite_note-Parker_Kim_Sutter_Carlson_2004_pp._1160–1164-14) Due to the high intelligence of the breed it requires a lot of exercise and stimulation. Insufficient exercise may lead to anxiety which leads to undesirable behaviours, notably the "shiba scream".[[11]](#cite_note-Spruce-11)[[9]](#cite_note-PetMD-9) The Shiba Inu has a reputation for being "aloof" and early socialization as a puppy is key for the dog to get along with other people and animals.[[15]](#cite_note-15)

A survey in Japan found the Shiba Inu to be more likely to engage in destructive behaviour, refusal to walk whilst on a lead, engage in [mounting](/wiki/Copulation_(zoology) "Copulation (zoology)") behaviour, and tail chasing. fanoutqa_018072.x:
History of mobile phones :: Emergence of automated services :: chunk_0009
The first fully automated mobile phone system for vehicles was launched in Sweden in 1956. Named [MTA](/wiki/MTD_(mobile_network) "MTD (mobile network)") (Mobiltelefonisystem A), it allowed calls to be made and received in the car using a [rotary dial](/wiki/Rotary_dial "Rotary dial"). The car phone could also be paged. Calls from the car were direct dial, whereas incoming calls required an operator to locate the nearest base station to the car. It was developed by Sture Laurén and other engineers at [Televerket](/wiki/Televerket_(Sweden) "Televerket (Sweden)") network operator. [Ericsson](/wiki/Ericsson "Ericsson") provided the switchboard while Svenska Radioaktiebolaget (SRA) and [Marconi](/wiki/Marconi_Company "Marconi Company") provided the telephones and base station equipment. MTA phones consisted of [vacuum tubes](/wiki/Vacuum_tube "Vacuum tube") and [relays](/wiki/Relay "Relay"), and weighed 40 kilograms (88 lb). In 1962, an upgraded version called *Mobile System B (MTB)* was introduced. This was a [push-button telephone](/wiki/Push-button_telephone "Push-button telephone"), and used [transistors](/wiki/Transistors "Transistors") and [DTMF](/wiki/DTMF "DTMF") signaling to improve its operational reliability. In 1971 the [MTD](/wiki/MTD_(mobile_network) "MTD (mobile network)") version was launched, opening for several different brands of equipment and gaining commercial success.[[26]](#cite_note-26)[[27]](#cite_note-27) The network remained open until 1983 and still had 600 customers when it closed.

In 1958, development began on a similar system for motorists in the USSR named "[Altay](/wiki/Altai_(mobile_telephone_system) "Altai (mobile telephone system)")".[[28]](#cite_note-28) The main developers of the Altay system were the Voronezh Science Research Institute of Communications (VNIIS) and the State Specialized Project Institute (GSPI). In 1963, the service started in Moscow, and by 1970, was deployed in 30 cities across the USSR. Versions of the Altay system are still in use today as a [trunking system](/wiki/Trunked_radio_system "Trunked radio system") in some parts of Russia.

The main legal acts of the European Union come in three forms: [regulations](/wiki/Regulation_(European_Union) "Regulation (European Union)"), [directives](/wiki/Directive_(European_Union) "Directive (European Union)"), and [decisions](/wiki/Decision_(European_Union) "Decision (European Union)"). Regulations become law in all member states the moment they come into force, without the requirement for any implementing measures,[[k]](#cite_note-147) and automatically override conflicting domestic provisions.[[129]](#cite_note-art249-144) Directives require member states to achieve a certain result while leaving them discretion as to how to achieve the result. The details of how they are to be implemented are left to member states.[[l]](#cite_note-148) When the time limit for implementing directives passes, they may, under certain conditions, have [direct effect](/wiki/Direct_effect "Direct effect") in national law against member states. Decisions offer an alternative to the two above modes of legislation. They are legal acts which only apply to specified individuals, companies or a particular member state. They are most often used in [competition law](/wiki/Competition_law "Competition law"), or on rulings on [State Aid](/wiki/State_aid_(European_Union) "State aid (European Union)"), but are also frequently used for procedural or administrative matters within the institutions. Regulations, directives, and decisions are of equal legal value and apply without any formal hierarchy.[[131]](#cite_note-149)
